== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:
   - If `Retrieval status` is `not_accessible` (or the paper text below says `[FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE]`), you MUST set `paper_read = "not accessible"`, `study_design_identified = "cannot_tell (full text not accessible)"`, `chosen_tool = "cannot_tell"`, `why_tool_chosen = "full text not accessible"`, `overall_rating = "cannot_tell"`, `domain_ratings = []`, all 7 `cross_tool_domains` fields to `"cannot_tell"`, `overall_narrative_summary = "Full text not accessible; no risk-of-bias appraisal performed."`, `where_found_summary = "not accessible"`, and `evidence_quotes = []`. NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell: No human or household panel is followed over time; potential archival survival bias or gaps in municipal and corporate records across 1867–1967 are not audited.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern for causal attribution (narratively acknowledged): Although the narrative discusses concurrent shocks—rapid interwar and post-war immigration, the 1914 typhoid epidemic, World War I, the Spanish Civil War, Francoist autarchy, power outages, and the 1945–1953 drought—there is no counterfactual or statistical control to isolate institutional effects.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (narrative archival level): Traces concrete legal, regulatory, and contractual mechanisms—royal concessions (1824), the 1859 Eixample plan approval, 1891 municipal continuous-circulation sewer ordinances, failed municipalization negotiations, the 1925 Municipal Health Regulations Royal Decree vs landlord trickle-feed contracts, and the April 1950 Ter River transfer decree—via municipal and utility archives, but summarizes legal rules narratively without formal statutory coding or complete official gazette citations.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Quantitative supply and per-capita consumption indicators are assembled across heterogeneous historical estimates and private utility (SGAB) records without standardized definitions, independent verification of private well extraction, leakage adjustments, or clear population denominators.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate / Mixed: Reports concrete aggregate supply metrics (m3/day, plomes, litres per inhabitant per day, 1859 sewer inspection shares, 1910–1945 SGAB demand curve in Figure 1, and 1950–1974 source-disaggregated supply in Figure 2), but household-level access, spatial inequality, and sanitary conditions rely on illustrative qualitative accounts rather than systematic citywide microdata.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: Lacks a pre-specified protocol, formal Methods section, or exhaustive archival inventory, creating risk of selective emphasis in choosing illustrative archival dossiers, department store catalogues, and corporate utility reports.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern / Weak transparency: Purposive single-city historical case study (Barcelona, 1867–1967) using selected municipal files, contemporary hygiene treatises, and corporate utility archives without a documented archival sampling strategy or explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria.

domain_ratings.justification: Cites specific primary municipal archival dossiers and commission reports (AMCB, AHCB, Fundacion AGBAR Fonds) alongside key regulatory milestones—including the 1791 fee system, 1824 royal concession, 1859 Eixample approval, 1891 sanitation ordinances, 1920 French capital repatriation laws, 1925 Municipal Health Regulations Royal Decree, and April 1950 Ter River decree—though formal statutory titles and official gazette references are often summarized narratively rather than cited in full legal form.

Clearly distinguishes institutional authority and territorial scope across Barcelona's walled Old Town, the 1859 Eixample expansion, neighbouring municipalities prior to their 1897 annexation (e.g., Gracia, Sant Gervasi), peripheral working-class districts, Barcelona City Council, the Hydrographic Confederation of the Eastern Pyrenees, Crown Property, and the Spanish national government / Ministry of Public Works over 1867–1967.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 4–12, 16–18, 20 (all main sections and Conclusion)

domain_ratings.justification: Substantively characterizes the institutional, fiscal, and contractual regimes governing water and sanitation—municipal underfunding, private concession consolidation under SGAB's de facto monopoly, 1891 continuous-circulation sewer mandates, landlord trickle-feed contracts vs metered supply, and post-1950 surface-water transfer projects—though framed narratively rather than as formally operationalized variables.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 5–7, 10–12, 16–18, 20 (sections on Eixample, sanitation, SGAB monopoly, domestic sphere, and post-war restrictions)

domain_ratings.justification: Tracks transition outcomes using identifiable physical and institutional indicators—daily flow volumes (plomes and m3/day), per-capita supply (litres/person/day), early customer counts (1873), 1859 street sewer coverage/condition shares, rationing hours (30% cut in May 1953), and source-specific supply trajectories (1950–1974)—while domestic adoption across social classes is defined qualitatively through fixture ownership and persistence of public bath/wash-houses.

Contains no dedicated Methods section or archival search protocol explaining how specific dossiers in AMCB, AHCB, and Fundacion AGBAR Fonds, or illustrative contemporary publications, were sampled from the universe of surviving municipal and corporate records.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Guardia, Rossello, and Garriga (2014) present a single-city archival institutional and urban-historical case study of Barcelona's century-long transition to a modern domestic water and sanitation system (1867–1967). Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (structured non-validated judgment; no numeric score), the study demonstrates strong jurisdictional specificity and rich institutional contextualization—tracing municipal fiscal limits, private utility consolidation under SGAB, sanitary ordinances (1891), failed municipalization bids, landlord trickle-feed contracts undermining the 1925 Royal Decree on water metering, and post-1950 surface-water catchments from the Llobregat and Ter rivers—supported by traceable archival call numbers (AMCB, AHCB, Fundacion AGBAR Fonds). However, as a traditional humanities narrative with no Methods section, it exhibits weak sampling, selection, and measurement transparency (relying on purposively chosen dossiers and unverified corporate/municipal flow statistics), lacks formal source-bias reflexivity toward private utility records, and supports causal claims solely through chronological narrative rather than counterfactual identification.
raw_response.overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Adequate institutional-archival contextualization, but weak sampling, measurement, and causal-identification rigour (no numeric composite score)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Archival institutional and legal-historical single-case study (narrative urban history with descriptive historical utility statistics, 1867–1967)
raw_response.where_found_summary: No standalone Methods section is present (humanities historical article). Study scope and thesis appear in the Abstract and first section (PDF pp. 2–5); archival municipal, regulatory, and corporate evidence is cited in footnotes and narrative sections across PDF pp. 4–21 (AMCB, AHCB, Fundacion AGBAR Fonds); descriptive quantitative water demand and provenance series appear in Figure 1 (PDF p. 15) and Figure 2 (PDF p. 19).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The article is an archival urban, institutional, and legal-historical single-case study of Barcelona (1867–1967) without a comparator unit (ruling out ROBINS-I), without an analytical cross-sectional or cohort sample (ruling out JBI checklists), and without human-participant qualitative fieldwork such as interviews, focus groups, or ethnography (making CASP and MMAT ill-fitting). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1–2, the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is specifically designated for institutional/legal-historical case studies that fit none of the conventional empirical designs.
